title: Analysis of MILP techniques for the pooling problem
contribution: Proves that every piecewise-linear MILP relaxation of the pooling problem is within a tight factor n (number of outputs) of the optimum, that beating n^(1-eps) in polynomial time is unlikely, and turns the proof's construction into a guaranteed MILP restriction that beats BARON and local solvers on large instances.
problem_entry: Empirical evidence that piecewise-linear MILP relaxations give good pooling bounds but no formal quality result (abstract p. 1, p. 5); defines a whole relaxation-scheme class (Def. 1, p. 4).
key_idea: Relax the pq-relaxation to IPOP by deleting q; routing all flow to the best single output restores consistency, giving ratio n and an LP-based n-approximation that is then enlarged into a pool-splitting MILP restriction PQ(tau, lambda) (pp. 7-8, 12, 14-16).
assumptions: Standard pooling (no pool-pool arcs), maximization with z*>0, consistent capacities WLOG (p. 2); hardness assumes NP-complete problems lack randomized polytime algorithms (Thm. 3, p. 12).
proof_devices: IPOP relaxation-of-relaxation plus keep-one-output rounding, checked constraint by constraint (pp. 7-8)
finite-slope argument for tightness over every piecewise-linear scheme; two-pool n-output instance with z*=1 and relaxation value n-eps (Prop. 2, pp. 8-11)
approximation-factor-preserving reading of the Alfaki-Haugland stable-set reduction plus Hastad (Prop. 3, Thm. 2, pp. 12-13)
ratio v_ilj/y_lj independent of j recovers q for validity of the restriction (eqs. (18)-(19), p. 17)
multiples-of-1/kappa rationality argument for tightness of the MILP restriction (Claim 7, pp. 17-18)
stable-set-derived bad family with z*/z_U(tau) = n'/tau (Prop. 5, p. 20)
experiments: U(tau), A(tau) MILP restrictions (Cplex 1 h, feasibility emphasis) vs BARON 6 h, SNOPT, SLP, alternating LP, FlowAug on 20 std* + 50 self-generated random instances; % gap to BARON dual bound, performance profiles overall and for n>=30, geometric means by n (pp. 21-26, App. B-D).
positioning: Explains the computational PL-relaxation literature (Gounaris-Misener-Floudas etc.) rather than competing with it; reuses and strengthens Alfaki-Haugland's NP-hardness reduction (pp. 3-5, 12).
writing: Overview of Results section before proofs (pp. 5-6); two-sided theorems; immediate defence of the weak-looking factor n (p. 6); numbered open questions (pp. 27-28).
limits_future: Practice far better than the tight factor n (p. 28); restrictions for different discretizations incomparable (p. 19); bad family (p. 20); open: complexity for fixed specs or bounded out-degree, better-than-n restrictions, polyhedral/symmetry study (pp. 27-29).

transferable: Bound every refinement of a relaxation by dropping the coupling variables and recovering a feasible point with a loss factor (IPOP, pp. 7-8)

Check that an existing NP-hardness reduction is approximation-factor preserving to obtain inapproximability (p. 13)
Design a MILP restriction that provably contains an approximation algorithm's outputs so the heuristic inherits the guarantee (Thm. 4, p. 16)
Report gaps to the global solver's dual bound, split profiles by instance size and average by the theorem's parameter n (pp. 25-26)

quotes.text: However in the worst case, these arbitrarily small errors in each bilinear term can propagate and lead to an overall error of approximately n for the entire piecewise linear MILP relaxation.

If we view the performance of the MILP based restriction of the pooling problem proposed in this paper on its own, we observe that the quality of solutions that are produced by MILP are significantly better than the theoretical performance guarantee of n.

title: Forbidden vertices
contribution: Introduces the forbidden-vertices problem (optimise over the vertices of a polytope minus a given set), classifies its complexity by the encodings of P and X, gives compact extended formulations and polynomial algorithms for tractable 0-1 and box-integral polytopes, and applies them to k-best solutions and binary all-different problems.
problem_entry: Need from enumerative schemes for stochastic integer programs that discard evaluated solutions, plus the link to k-best basic solutions; complexity made a function of explicit vs implicit encodings of P and X (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Encoding decides complexity; for 0-1 polytopes cover {0,1}^n minus X by at most n|X| cube faces (longest common prefixes) and optimise, or take the disjunctive hull, over P intersected with each face (Def. 14, Props. 15-17, Thm. 16, p. 8).
assumptions: Rational polytopes; tractable = polytime separation oracle; positive results need 0-1 vertices or box-integrality, which the authors call crucial (pp. 1-2, 9, 12).
proof_devices: polarity example: removing one vertex raises the facet count from n^2+1 to 2^n (Prop. 5, p. 3)
forb(P,X) as the hull of the union of faces avoiding X, giving f(P)^(|X|+1) (Prop. 6, p. 3)
simplex-path connectivity of upper level sets for independent removals, with a simplex counterexample to the converse (Prop. 7, pp. 3-4)
sandwich hardness: cut polytope plus scaled unit vectors (Thm. 9, pp. 4-5) and TSP tours between edge-count layers (Thm. 18, pp. 9-10), with extension-complexity lower bounds
reductions from knapsack, the 'another vertex' decision problem and vertex cover (Prop. 10 p. 5, Thm. 11 pp. 5-6, Prop. 20 p. 10)
binary-expansion bijection and recursive projection for O(n|X|) extended formulations of the cube case (pp. 6-7)
exchange argument reducing all-different to a min-weight R-matching over k-best lists (Thm. 24, p. 12)
positioning: Generalises Lee's cropped-cubes result, re-derives Lawler's k-best tractability, answers an open question of Lee's all-different paper; uses Fiorini et al., Rothvoss, Khachiyan et al., Boros et al. as tools (pp. 4-6, 9, 11).
writing: Contribution bullets plus a classification table with a theorem per cell and an explicitly unresolved cell (p. 2); intuition sentences before refinements and a warning against a tempting converse (pp. 3-4).
limits_future: Complexity of explicit P with X a facet left open, with a TU tractable subclass (pp. 2, 10); removing a list of faces is hard (p. 10); integral-case k-best/all-different claims stated without proof (p. 14); no future-work section.

method_links.note: Each tractable case paired with hardness when one hypothesis (encoding of P, encoding of X, 0-1 vertices) is dropped; the open cell is marked as open

title: Approximating polyhedra with sparse inequalities
contribution: Defines the distance between a polytope and its k-sparse closure as a measure of what sparse cuts lose, proves vertex-count upper bounds (half sparsity suffices with polynomially many vertices), near-matching lower bounds for random 0/1 polytopes, a negative result for hard packing IPs, and that sparse cuts in extended spaces are never worse and can be much better.
problem_entry: Solvers use sparsity as a cut-selection criterion because dense cuts slow LPs, yet very few studies exist; the two-sided trade-off is cut to one side: how much gap closure is lost using only k-sparse cuts (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Study P^k (intersection of all valid k-sparse cuts) through d(P,P^k), chosen after rejecting objective and volume ratios; bound it by sparsifying the separating hyperplane through randomized rounding (pp. 2-3, 7-9).
assumptions: Polytopes in [0,1]^n WLOG; upper bounds deterministic in the vertex count; lower bounds probabilistic for uniform random 0/1 points in a parameter window and for the (n,m,M)-PIP distribution; constants not optimised (pp. 2, 5-6).
proof_devices: projection separating hyperplane, then randomized rounding of its normal, with Bernstein for sparsity and validity and Markov for separation (Lemma 1, Claims 1-3, pp. 7-9)
averaging the k-sparse relaxations of one halfspace over all k-subsets (Lemma 2, pp. 9-10)
alpha-tough polytopes and a new anticoncentration lemma for Bernoulli sums far from the standard deviation, proved by bucketing and trimming (Def. 1 p. 10, Lemma 3 p. 11, App. C pp. 19-20)
finite set of integral facet normals of 0/1 polytopes to enable a union bound (Lemmas 4-6, pp. 11-12)
aggregated near-uniform cut, order statistics, and randomized rounding plus averaging into the integer hull for packing IPs (Lemmas 9-13, pp. 13-15)
binary-tree extended formulation with 3-sparse constraints (Prop. 2, p. 17)
experiments: Small exact computation only: n=10, 150 random binary points, PORTA facet descriptions plus a shooting experiment over 20,000 random directions for lower bounds on d(P,P^k); larger sizes not possible (p. 4, App. B pp. 18-19).
positioning: Claims near-absence of prior study (only Andersen-Weismantel zero-coefficient cuts and single-row cuts); evidence for the practice from solver-developer personal communications; follow-up lower-bound paper cited (pp. 1-2, 18, 21-22).
writing: Motivation, reasoned choice of measure with counterexamples, four contrasting examples, then a Main Results section with regime-by-regime interpretation before the proofs (pp. 1-7).
limits_future: Theorem 1 only captures the worst case and is not tight for Example 4; the lower bound holds with probability 1/4 in a window (p. 5); future: IP-style ratio measures, computational experiments, packing IPs with sparse LP formulations (p. 18).
